title: Why Did South San Change How Teachers Teach?
subtitles: Were Teachers Really What South San Needed to Fix? — Part 1
excerpt: TEA replaced South San’s elected Board primarily to address longstanding governance and management problems. Yet less than two months later, the new Board moved to substantially restructure classroom instruction districtwide by approving NIET/TAP, a management-style model that shifts instructional decision-making toward district-directed expectations and monitoring. What is NIET/TAP—and was deficient teaching really a significant enough problem at South San to warrant such a rapid districtwide restructuring of classroom instruction?

sections.content: A Bit of Background: Why Did TEA Replace South San’s Board?

On February 19, 2025, TEA replaced South San’s elected Board of Trustees with a seven-member Board of Managers after years of documented governance problems, financial-control concerns, and repeated state investigations. TEA’s stated reasons for the intervention centered primarily on longstanding problems with district governance and management.

Two months later, on April 14, 2025, the newly installed Board of Managers, acting on the superintendent’s recommendation, approved districtwide implementation of NIET/TAP, a school-improvement  model developed outside the district.
What Is NIET/TAP?

TAP (The System for Teacher and Student Advancement) was introduced in 1999 by Lowell Milken, whose professional background was in law, business, and philanthropy rather than classroom teaching. He later founded the National Institute for Excellence in Teaching (NIET).

NIET/TAP uses prescribed instructional practices, professional development, coaching, observation, evaluation, accountability, and performance measures to move classroom practice toward the model’s expectations. NIET describes its rubric as defining effective teaching and creating a common language and vision for instruction. The model also includes performance-based compensation tied to teacher roles, classroom performance, and student performance.

“They would help us establish protocols for PLCs, establish protocols of how to evaluate teachers, establish protocols of how to evaluate master teachers.” — Dr. Saul Hinojosa, April 14, 2025 Board meeting
But South San Already Has Standards and Teacher Evaluation Systems

South San already operates within common academic standards and an established system for evaluating teachers. The TEKS establish what Texas students are expected to know and be able to do. T-TESS provides a common statewide framework for defining and evaluating effective teaching, and South San also has a Teacher Incentive Allotment system that uses teacher-observation and student-growth measures in determining teacher designations and incentive funding.

Already in place before districtwide NIET/TAP:[Make Bullets] TEKS - what students are expected to learnT-TESS - common framework for evaluating teachingTIA - evaluation system linking teacher observation, student growth, and incentive funding

NIET/TAP therefore does not create academic standards, teacher evaluation, feedback, or performance incentives; those already exist. It adds a more intensive system for defining, coaching, observing, evaluating, and eventually rewarding instructional practice. And unlike South San’s earlier TIA development process, we have not found evidence in the public materials we reviewed that classroom teachers had a comparable role in deciding whether or how NIET/TAP would be adopted districtwide.
How is NIET/TAP changing teaching in South San classrooms?

At South San, the decision changed both how teachers were expected to teach and how their teaching would be monitored and evaluated. Under NIET/TAP, teachers are coached, observed, and evaluated against a detailed instructional rubric. NIET/TAP was also implemented alongside broader district curriculum requirements that affected the materials teachers could use and how much latitude they had to adapt instruction to differences among students.

But common learning expectations do not require identical instruction. Different students, classes, subjects, and circumstances require different explanations, pacing, grouping, materials, or approaches. Variation in instruction can benefit students because it allows teachers to respond to what is actually happening in the classroom rather than following the same approach regardless of student need.
Common learning expectations do not require identical instruction—and greater uniformity in instruction does not, by itself, mean better instruction.

NIET/TAP represents a significant shift in who directs day-to-day instruction. Instead of teachers primarily deciding how best to teach the required standards, instructional practice is increasingly shaped by NIET/TAP’s defined expectations and reinforced through district-directed training, coaching, observation, and evaluation. NIET/TAP may call for teachers to respond to student needs, but it also defines and evaluates what effective instructional practice should look like. That shifts more authority over how teachers respond to students from the classroom teacher toward the system evaluating the teacher.
What Does This Mean for Students?

Much of the real work of education happens in the moments when teachers use their knowledge, experience, creativity, and relationships with students to respond to what a class or an individual student needs. A teacher may need to slow down, explain something differently, abandon a planned activity, provide more practice, challenge students who are ready to move ahead, or take an approach that was not anticipated in advance. When teachers have less freedom to make those judgments, students may also lose some of the flexibility, creativity, individual attention, and responsiveness that can help them learn, stay engaged, and succeed.

Moving from a system in which teachers exercise substantial professional judgment over how to teach their students to one in which district-prescribed expectations increasingly define and monitor instructional practice is a significant shift. It changes not only how teachers are evaluated, but also who controls day-to-day instructional decisions.
The concern is not whether teachers should respond to student needs. It is who decides what that response should look like—the teacher in the classroom, or the system evaluating the teacher?

The issue is not whether teachers should respond to student needs—of course they should. The concern is who decides what that response should look like. Under NIET/TAP, teachers are trained and coached toward defined instructional practices and then observed and evaluated against that same framework. A teacher may be exercising professional judgment in response to students, but if the evaluator determines that the observed practice does not meet the rubric’s expectations, that judgment can result in a lower evaluation score. The system therefore does more than support teachers in responding to students; it also judges whether they responded in the way the framework defines as effective.

So why did South San make such a significant shift in instructional decision-making when academic standards, teacher evaluation, professional development, and teacher supports were already in place? Before restructuring teaching districtwide, was there evidence that deficiencies in teacher practice were serious, widespread, and a significant contributor to low student performance?
Read Part 2 as we look at what evidence South San actually had about the quality of teaching before adopting NIET/TAP districtwide—and what that evidence really showed.

title: Where Is the Root-Cause Analysis?
subtitles: Were Teachers Really What South San Needed to Fix? — Part 3
excerpt: Four months after South San approved districtwide NIET/TAP, the administration presented what was described as its “data analysis and root cause.” The PowerPoint itself is not visible in the public meeting video or among the workshop materials we located, but the discussion identifies the kinds of data the administration said it reviewed. We followed those sources and later district records to see what can be reconstructed—and what remains unclear about the evidence behind the administration’s conclusions.

sections.content: New to the series? Read [Part 1] and [Part 2].
In [Part 2], we followed the public record through the April 14, 2025 vote to approve districtwide NIET/TAP. The timeline below follows what happened next.
What Happened After the April 14 Vote?
[View the complete South San NIET/TAP timeline.]

Recall that in [Part 2], we learned that TEA Conservator Abe Saavedra had promised a new Needs Assessment, which would be conducted over the following several weeks and presented to the Board. Saavedra said the assessment would be used to identify TEA exit-criteria goals—the goals and conditions tied to the district’s eventual transition back to elected governance. Yet districtwide NIET/TAP was approved that same night, before the new assessment had been completed. The public materials for that vote did not include South San-specific analysis showing that problems in teaching practice were a significant contributor to low student performance across the district.
What Happened at the August 25 Workshop?

Four months later, at the [August 25 workshop], Board coach Ben Mackey described three separate inputs for the Board’s priority-setting work: the Corrective Action Plan, TEA exit criteria, and a “root cause and data analysis” conducted by the superintendent and his team. Hinojosa and his team presented what was described as their “data analysis and root cause.”

During the workshop, Hinojosa asked for a “PowerPoint presentation,” and participants repeatedly referred to and moved among slides while discussing the administration's analysis. But the presentation itself is not shown in the public workshop video we reviewed. We can hear participants referring to and moving between slides, but the viewer never sees them. We also did not locate the presentation among the publicly posted workshop materials.
So Where Was the PowerPoint?

Nearly a year later, in late August 2026, South San AFT—the local affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers—submitted a public-records request for “a copy of the PowerPoint on Data Analysis and Root Causes presented by Dr. Hinojosa at the August 25, 2025 Board of Managers special session.” The district responded by sending the same two documents already publicly posted for the workshop—the Draft Implementation Plan and Corrective Action Plan/Exit Criteria—and stated: “There were no PowerPoints”, even though a PowerPoint is clearly referred to in the workshop video.
So We Tried to Reconstruct the Missing Data

Since the PowerPoint was not shown in the public workshop video and the district later denied its existence, we tried another approach. Hinojosa listed several [kinds of records] his team had reviewed, so we looked for public information about the ones he identified that related to teachers and teaching:

[Make into bullets]Walkthroughs: Hinojosa said the district had conducted about 3,500 walkthroughs during the previous three months and used them to identify who they considered “quality educators” and who they did not. We have not found a public districtwide summary showing how many teachers were identified as having problems, what those problems were, what criteria were used, or how widespread the problems were.Teacher evaluations: We have not found public districtwide results showing how teachers were rated or how many fell below expectations.Cluster evaluations: We have not found public results showing what they revealed about teaching practice across the district.Teacher attendance: This may tell us something about staffing stability and continuity for students, but it does not tell us whether teachers were ineffective in the classroom.

So far, we can see what kinds of teacher-related information the district said it reviewed, but not what those records actually showed about the extent of problems with teaching. The public record therefore still leaves some important questions unresolved. Why isn’t the presentation visible in the public workshop video? Why wasn’t it included with the posted workshop materials? And why, when South San AFT specifically requested the PowerPoint discussed during the meeting, did the district respond that there were no PowerPoints?

To see whether the Board members could provide answers, on September 8, 2026, we sent [questions] individually to each member asking what role they personally played in reviewing the evidence, what South San-specific evidence they reviewed before approving districtwide NIET/TAP, whether the promised Needs Assessment or root-cause analysis was completed, and where the public can review that evidence.
As of October 1, 2026, no responses had been received from any of the Board Managers. [Check here] to see whether any responses have been received since then.
Why Does the Missing Presentation Matter?

Districtwide NIET/TAP had already been approved for four months. So why was the administration only now presenting its data analysis and root-cause work? One of the recommendations discussed was to “invest in teacher capacity.” The missing presentation could help show how the district moved from its data to that recommendation—and whether its analysis identified teacher-related factors as a significant contributor to low student performance.

Without the presentation, we cannot see what teacher-related evidence was shown, how strongly it supported the administration’s conclusions, or how those factors compared with other possible causes of low student performance.

The public record therefore leaves several questions unresolved. Why isn’t the presentation visible in the public workshop video? Why wasn’t it included with the posted workshop materials? And why, when South San AFT specifically requested the PowerPoint discussed during the meeting, did the district respond that there were no PowerPoints?
Why the Evidence Matters

NIET/TAP was not a minor change. It involved additional costs, changed how teachers are trained, coached, observed, and evaluated, and shifted more instructional decision-making from individual teachers toward district-directed expectations and practices.

For a decision of that scale, the public should be able to review the underlying data and analysis—with personal or identifying information removed where necessary—so they can evaluate whether the evidence supports the district’s conclusions.
So WERE teachers really what South San needed to fix?

Based on the public record we have been able to review, we still cannot answer that question. The August presentation may contain information that would help, but we cannot evaluate evidence we cannot see. Until the underlying analysis is available for public review—or additional evidence is provided—we cannot independently determine whether the evidence supported making deficiencies in teaching practice such a significant focus of South San’s improvement strategy.
What Can You Do?

[Make into Bullets]Ask district leaders. Contact the [Superintendent] and [Board of Managers] and ask whether the promised Needs Assessment was completed and where the Needs Assessment, root-cause analysis, and August 25 presentation can be reviewed.Request the records. If the documents are not publicly available, [submit a public-information request] to South San.Share what you find. If you receive a response or document that helps answer these questions, [contact South San Education Explained] so we can review it an

title: Was There Evidence That Teaching Was a Significant Problem at South San?
subtitles: Were Teachers Really What South San Needed to Fix? — Part 2
excerpt: Before South San’s Board of Managers approved districtwide NIET/TAP on April 14, 2025, what evidence showed that deficiencies in teaching practice were a major cause of low student performance? This article follows the timeline of what the district had identified, what was presented before the vote, what was still being studied, and what remains unclear about the evidence behind the decision.

sections.content: If you haven’t read Part 1, start here.

In an effort to improve student performance, South San adopted NIET/TAP, a model that puts changing teacher practice at the center of its improvement strategy. Teachers are trained, coached, observed, and evaluated against prescribed instructional practices. But before we ask whether NIET/TAP was the right solution, we need to ask a more basic question:
Did problems in teaching practice contribute significantly to South San's low student performance?

To answer that, we went back to the period before Superintendent Hinojosa arrived and before TEA appointed the new Board of Managers. We looked at what South San itself had already identified as its major needs and challenges, then followed the public record forward to see what changed, what evidence was presented, and when.
South San NIET/TAP Timeline
What the Timeline Shows So Far

We started by looking for South San’s March 2024 Comprehensive Needs Assessment. The district’s original PDF is no longer available at its former web address, but search engines still retain indexed text captured when the document was publicly available.
That text identifies teacher turnover as the formal staff-quality concern. It does not appear identify deficiencies in teaching practice as a districtwide root cause of low student performance. Other identified needs included learning loss, curriculum and intervention systems, data use, and related district processes.
We are considering submitting a public-information request to obtain the complete assessment and verify these findings.
In October 2024, South San approved limited NIET support for four campuses. That earlier agreement was substantially different from the districtwide NIET/TAP system proposed and implemented in 2025.

Then, at the April 14, 2025 Board meeting, TEA Conservator Abe Saavedra told the Board that a [new Needs Assessment] would be conducted over the following several weeks, presented to the Board, and used to identify TEA “exit criteria” goals — the specific goals and conditions the district and Board of Managers must meet before control can transition back to an elected board.

Hinojosa [described NIET/TAP] based on his experience in his previous district, including procedures for professional learning communities, teacher evaluations, and performance-based pay. He did not present South San-specific analysis demonstrating that problems in teaching practice were a significant contributor to low student performance across the district or that South San needed this kind of intervention.

One Board member [referred to reviewing materials] but did not specify which materials or when they were reviewed. They praised individualized campus support and what they called "strength-based coaching." However, that term does not fully describe NIET/TAP's approach, which also identifies areas needing improvement and uses observations and evaluations to monitor teachers' compliance with prescribed instructional practices. The member did not explain how individual campus needs would be identified or how this support would improve student learning.
After that comment, Hinojosa formally recommended approval. A motion and second followed. The chair invited [further discussion or questions]; none followed, and the Board approved the proposal 7–0.
What Had the Board Considered Before the Vote?

To better understand what evidence the Board had reviewed before the April 14 vote, we examined its public meeting calendar and posted meeting records. We found no public record of earlier Board consideration of districtwide NIET/TAP.
What Was in the Board Packet?

The public meeting agenda lists one NIET/TAP attachment: an eight-page document containing the agenda summary and NIET's Statement of Work for districtwide TAP support at 12 schools, totaling $252,500. Under "Historical Data," the summary states "none." The document does not analyze the potential effects on teachers' workload, instructional discretion, or student learning.

We found no South San-specific data showing how widespread problems with teaching were, no analysis connecting those problems to low student performance, and no root-cause analysis identifying teaching practice as a significant contributor to the district’s academic results.
So where was the evidence supporting such a significant districtwide restructuring of instruction?

So far, we’ve determined:[Make into Bullets]
Saavedra’s Needs Assessment for developing TEA exit-criteria goals had not been completed when the Board voted to implement NIET/TAP, restructuring instruction districtwide.We found no public record of earlier Board consideration of districtwide NIET/TAP.
One Board member referred to reviewing unspecified materials and commented favorably on the program. No questions were asked, and its potential practical impacts were not examined in the public discussion. The public presentation and agenda attachment did not provide South San-specific analysis demonstrating that problems in teaching practice were a significant contributor to low student performance districtwide.

At that workshop, the corrective action plan, TEA exit criteria, and the superintendent’s “root cause and data analysis” were described as three separate inputs for setting district priorities. Hinojosa and his team presented what was described as their “data analysis and root cause.”
Was this where the missing evidence would appear—and what did the district’s root-cause analysis actually show?
Continue to [Part 3]: Where Is the Root-Cause Analysis?

title: Was There Evidence That Poor Teaching Was a Significant Problem at South San?
subtitles: Were Teachers Really What South San Needed to Fix? — Part 2
excerpt: Before South San’s Board of Managers approved districtwide NIET/TAP on April 14, 2025, what evidence showed that deficiencies in teaching practice were a major cause of low student performance? This article follows the timeline of what the district had identified, what was presented before the vote, what was still being studied, and what remains unclear about the evidence behind the decision.

sections.content: If you haven’t read Part 1, start here.

In an effort to improve student performance, South San adopted NIET/TAP, a model that puts changing teacher practice at the center of its improvement strategy. Teachers are trained, coached, observed, and evaluated against prescribed instructional practices. But before asking whether NIET/TAP was the right solution, there is a more basic question:
Was ineffective teaching actually a significant problem at South San?

To answer that, we went back to the period before Superintendent Hinojosa arrived and before TEA appointed the new Board of Managers. We looked at what South San itself had already identified as its major needs and challenges, then followed the public record forward to see what changed, what evidence was presented, and when.
South San NIET/TAP Timeline
What the Timeline Shows So Far

We started by looking for South San’s March 2024 Comprehensive Needs Assessment. The district’s original PDF is no longer available at its former web address, but search engines still retain indexed text captured when the document was publicly available.
That text identifies teacher turnover as the formal staff-quality concern. It does not appear identify deficiencies in teaching practice as a districtwide root cause of low student performance. Other identified needs included learning loss, curriculum and intervention systems, data use, and related district processes.

Then came April 14, 2025. TEA Conservator Abe Saavedra told the Board that “over the next several weeks” he would conduct a new Needs Assessment with Hinojosa and district staff. He said the completed assessment would be presented to the Board and used to identify specific goals for the district. At that same meeting—before that assessment had been completed—Hinojosa recommended districtwide implementation of NIET/TAP, and the Board of Managers approved it 7–0.
What Had the Board Considered Before the Vote?

In an effort to find evidence that the Board had examined districtwide NIET/TAP and evaluated it as a solution before April 14, we reviewed the Board’s public meeting calendar and posted meeting records leading up to the vote. We found no public record showing earlier Board consideration of districtwide NIET/TAP.

It is important to note that South San had worked with NIET previously in a limited capacity. That earlier involvement, however, was substantially different from the districtwide NIET/TAP system proposed and implemented in 2025.

So then we looked at what happened at the April 14 meeting itself. Hinojosa described NIET/TAP and asked whether Board members had any questions. No Board member asked a question about the proposal. After a motion and second, the chair again invited discussion or questions. None followed, and the Board approved districtwide NIET/TAP 7–0.
What Was in the Board Packet?

The official Board record includes an eight-page attachment for the April 14 NIET/TAP agenda item. It includes the agenda summary and NIET’s Statement of Work for districtwide TAP support at 12 schools, totaling $252,500. Under “Historical Data,” the summary states “none.”

We found no South San-specific data showing how widespread problems with teaching were, no analysis connecting those problems to low student performance, and no root-cause analysis identifying teaching practice as a significant contributor to the district’s academic results.
So where was the evidence supporting such a significant districtwide restructuring of instruction?

So far, we’ve determined:
• The new Needs Assessment had not been completed when the Board voted.
• We found no public record of earlier Board consideration of districtwide NIET/TAP.
• No Board member asked a question when the proposal came up for approval.
• The materials provided before the meeting contained no South San-specific analysis showing that problems with teaching were a significant contributor to low student performance.
Four months later, the Board met for an August 25 workshop. Hinojosa and his team presented what was described as their “data analysis and root cause.”
Was this where the missing evidence would appear—and what did the district’s root-cause analysis actually show?
